title: overlays
text:
All five components float above the page without changing its layout. Native popovers close on Escape or a click outside them (light dismiss). While a modal dialog is open, the browser marks the rest of the page inert. AnswerUI keeps those browser behaviours, applies a shared floating surface, and places popovers beside their opener. Dropdown menus use popovers. Tooltips use CSS anchor positioning instead of the Popover API.
from fasthtml.common import *
from answerui.demo import demo
from fastcore.test import *

title: overlays
text:
Popover
Popover renders a floating panel on the raised neutral surface (--color-surface). Set popovertarget on a button to open it. The browser closes the panel on Escape or a click outside it. While the panel is open, mountPopover sets aria-expanded="true" on the opener, and Btn displays its pressed style.
CSS anchor rules place the panel beside the opener and flip it when it would overflow the viewport. In browsers without anchor positioning, mountPopover computes coordinates in JavaScript and closes the panel if the opener leaves the viewport. Pass side ('bottom'), align ('start'), and side_offset (6 pixels) to configure initial placement. Popover emits popover, popup, data-side, data-align, and data-side-offset for mountPopover with no per-panel JavaScript.



Popover
def Popover(
    *c, popover:str='auto', side:str='bottom', align:str='start', side_offset:int=6, **attrs
):
A native popover positioned beside its opener by the shared controller


The shared stylesheet sets the floating surface, viewport size limits, and entry animation. The browser’s Popover API handles hiding, light dismiss, and focus restoration.
Set popovertarget on any button to the popover’s id to open it. Put ordinary HTML content inside the panel:

Popover.demo(height='9rem')


  
↻

title: overlays
text:
Dropdown
Dropdown returns a (trigger, panel) pair containing a button trigger and a native popover of links, buttons, separators, and supplementary content. Pass a label string to create a secondary Btn trigger, or pass a configured Btn to control its variant and attributes. Give an icon-only trigger an accessible name such as aria_label. Dropdown always sets type='button' on the trigger so it never submits an enclosing form.
Dropdown items are ordinary HTML links and buttons rather than an ARIA role="menu" widget. Users move between them with Tab and Shift+Tab, skipping disabled buttons. When the panel opens, mountPopover focuses the first enabled visible control inside it. Dropdown adds menu-item to each direct a and button child and sets popovertarget and popovertargetaction='hide' on buttons that do not already have a popovertarget. Clicking a link with href closes the panel in mountPopover. The browser handles Escape and light dismiss. To mark an unavailable item, set disabled=True on a button or omit href on a link.



Dropdown
def Dropdown(
    trigger, *items, id:NoneType=None, **attrs
):
A button and its native popover of ordinary links and actions


The Account example uses a text trigger and starts with the user’s name and email aligned with its items. The Options example passes a configured Btn with aria_label. Tabbing through the items skips both the static header text and the disabled Duplicate button:

Dropdown.demo(height='14rem')


  
↻

title: overlays
text:
Invoker commands
Set commandfor on a button to a dialog’s id and command to 'show-modal' or 'close'. In browsers without native Invoker Commands support, the shared click handler in browser.js calls showModal() or close() on the target dialog. Use popovertarget for popovers.

title: overlays
text:
Dialog
Dialog renders a native <dialog> element with dialog and dialog-side attributes. Open it as a modal with command='show-modal' and commandfor. The browser moves focus into the dialog, closes it on Escape, and marks the rest of the page inert. Because the dialog stays in its DOM position while rendered in the top layer, it inherits its font and custom properties from its parent element. Close it with command='close' or a <form method="dialog">.
The shared stylesheet sets the floating surface (--color-surface), rounded corners (--radius1), entry animation (ui-dialog-enter), and backdrop tint. Add closedby='any' so a click on the backdrop closes the dialog. Omit closedby='any' on confirmations where the user must click a button.



Dialog
def Dialog(
    *c, side:str='center', **attrs
):
A native modal panel, or a full-height drawer at the start or end edge


The htmx listener in browser.js calls showModal() on a closed Dialog after htmx swaps content into a descendant inside it. A button that loads the dialog body with hx-get does not need command='show-modal'. Because the dialog opens after the swap finishes, users never see stale content. Swapping the <dialog> element itself does not open it. A server can send a closed <dialog> out of band to close an open one.
This confirmation dialog uses a Stack for its body and a Cluster for its action buttons. Set aria_labelledby to the heading’s id to give the dialog an accessible name. The browser does not derive a dialog’s accessible name from a nested heading:

Dialog.demo(height='16rem')


  
↻

title: overlays
text:
Drawer
Pass side='end' or side='start' to Dialog to place it against the inline edge of the viewport (right and left in left-to-right pages). The drawer uses --drawer-size (24rem by default) for its width and expands to 100vw on viewports narrower than 40rem. Tall content scrolls inside the drawer. A drawer opens and closes like a centred Dialog, with the same Escape and page-inertness behaviour. Add closedby='any' so a click outside closes the drawer in supporting browsers. A button with command='close' closes it in all browsers.

demo(Cluster(Btn('Filters', variant='secondary', command='show-modal', commandfor='filters'),
    Btn('Navigation', variant='secondary', command='show-modal', commandfor='nav-drawer'),
    Dialog(Stack(H2('Filters', id='filters-title'), P('Narrow the list.'),
        Btn('Done', command='close', commandfor='filters')),
        id='filters', aria_labelledby='filters-title', side='end', closedby='any'),
    Dialog(Stack(H2('Navigation', id='nav-title'), P('Sections of the app.'),
        Btn('Close', variant='secondary', command='close', commandfor='nav-drawer')),
        id='nav-drawer', aria_labelledby='nav-title', side='start', closedby='any')), height='12rem')


  
↻

title: overlays
text:
Tooltip
Tooltip pairs a control with a short supplementary description inside an inline span[tooltip]. It appends the description’s id to the control’s aria-describedby without overwriting existing IDs. Give the control its own accessible name because a tooltip never replaces a label. Use Popover for floating panels that contain interactive controls.
The description is real HTML shown by CSS alone. It appears immediately when the pointer is over the control or description, or when the control has keyboard focus (:focus-visible). Clicking the control does not show the tooltip. Once hover and keyboard focus end, the tooltip stays visible for 150ms and then fades out over --motion. You can move the pointer onto the description during that 150ms delay. Moving to another tooltip hides the first one immediately with no fade, matching native tooltips.
Tooltip links the control and description with inline anchor-name and position-anchor styles. With CSS anchor positioning, the browser centres the description above the control with a --tooltip-gap (6px default) gap and flips it below when there is no room above. In browsers without anchor positioning, the description is placed above the control and aligned to its left edge. Tooltips render outside the top layer rather than using the Popover API. An ancestor with transform or filter becomes the containing block and can clip the tooltip.



Tooltip
def Tooltip(
    trigger, text, id:NoneType=None, **attrs
):
A control and supplementary description shown by CSS on hover or keyboard focus



Tooltip.demo(height='7rem')


  
↻

title: answerui
text:
Use the @answerdotai/answerui npm package for the browser foundation: a stylesheet keyed on semantic HTML attributes and CSS custom properties, optional fonts, and vanilla JavaScript modules. Use the answerui-py Python package to add FastHTML constructors and a registry for app-specific CSS and browser behavior on top of those same assets.
Python constructors emit marked HTML, such as <section card> from Card() and <button btn> from Btn(). AnswerUI does not restyle unmarked form elements. Frontend frameworks such as Svelte can emit the same markup and import the JavaScript modules directly without Python. The notebooks cover the generated OKLCH palette, typography and spacing scales, parent-driven layouts, UI components, and the Python registry.
Read answerui.skill with doc(answerui.skill) for an LLM guide to building FastHTML pages, inspecting and customising registered components, and previewing results in a persistent Python kernel.

title: answerui
text:
Install
For a JavaScript app:
npm install @answerdotai/answerui
Import the stylesheet once:
import '@answerdotai/answerui/styles.css';
import {mountPopover} from '@answerdotai/answerui/floating.js';
@answerdotai/answerui/styles.css works without JavaScript, including native dialogs, disclosures, and CSS tooltips. Import individual browser modules only for components that require JavaScript: @answerdotai/answerui/floating.js for popovers, @answerdotai/answerui/fit.js for responsive navbars, @answerdotai/answerui/interactions.js for tabs, toolbars, and hover cards, and @answerdotai/answerui/copy.js for clipboard actions. Load @answerdotai/answerui/fonts.css to use the bundled IBM Plex font faces.
For server-rendered or static HTML, import '@answerdotai/answerui/browser.js' mounts those behaviors automatically on marked elements and observes later DOM insertions. In Svelte or another component framework, import the individual modules inside your component lifecycle instead of loading @answerdotai/answerui/browser.js.
For FastHTML:
pip install answerui-py
If you serve the browser assets directly from Python, from answerui import assets returns the packaged Path to the assets directory.

title: answerui
text:
Use from Python
reg.hdrs() returns the shared foundation stylesheet, browser scripts, and registered app rules. reg.ftrs() returns the fastlucide icon sprite sheet. Because FastHTML evaluates both on every response, newly registered rules take effect on the next request without a restart:

from fasthtml.common import *
from answerui.all import *


app = FastHTML(hdrs=reg.hdrs(), ftrs=reg.ftrs())
rt = app.route

To serve cached assets instead of inlining them on every page, create the app without reg.hdrs() or reg.ftrs(), then call reg.serve(app). That call registers the headers, icon sprite sheet, and content-hashed asset routes while preserving relative imports between the browser JavaScript modules.

served_app = FastHTML()
reg.serve(served_app);

Each Python constructor renders standard HTML with a semantic attribute. Below, Card renders <section card> and Stack wraps the children in <div stack> to space them vertically:

page = Card(Stack(H2('Profile'), Field('Name', Input(name='name')), Cluster(Btn('Save'), Btn('Cancel', variant='secondary'))))
demo(page)


  
↻  



demo(page) renders the Python markup with the same stylesheet and browser scripts used by JavaScript applications.

title: answerui
text:
Customise
Register standard CSS at the scope you want to change: :root custom properties via reg.rule for the whole app, a scoped selector for one region, or a component rule via Btn.rule. Because registered rules are placed in the app cascade layer after every framework layer except utilities, they override AnswerUI defaults without modifying the package:

reg.rule(':root { --hue: 150; --radius: 0; }', 'theme')
Btn.rule('caps', 'text-transform: uppercase;')

Btn.caps [app] [btn]


Call .variant() on a component to declare a named style modifier. The component constructor then accepts that variant name as a keyword argument. Declared variants also appear in the component’s documentation:

Btn.variant('cta', '--ui-pad-block: var(--space); --ui-pad-inline: var(--space2); font-size: var(--text1);', doc='The landing page call to action.')

Btn.cta [app] :is([btn])[cta]: The landing page call to action.


Declaring a variant registers an app-layer rule for that attribute on the component element without modifying the default styles in styles.css.

demo(Btn('Request access', cta=True))


  
↻  




Btn

Btn(*c, variant='primary', size=None, href=None, type='button', icon=False, **attrs)
A raised action, latched by aria-pressed and sunken while busy or expanded
Root selector: [btn].
Declared variants: - cta: The landing page call to action.
Rules: - base (app) - caps (app)

title: answerui
text:
Previews in notebooks
demo(page) returns a Preview with two MIME representations: an HTML iframe containing the full stylesheet and browser scripts, and a Markdown block of the HTML markup. Because each iframe embeds the entire stylesheet, committing them would bloat notebooks and churn diffs on every stylesheet edit. Preview._repr_mimebundle_ sets nbdev’s strip metadata flag on the HTML output. When you run nbdev-clean, it strips the iframe and keeps the Markdown markup in git. In a fresh clone, run the notebook cells to display the iframes again.
For the docs, set exec_all in pyproject.toml:
[tool.nbdev]
exec_all = true
nbdev-docs then executes every notebook and renders each iframe from the current code.

title: answerui
text:
With an LLM
answerui.skill is a pyskill whose module docstring documents how to use AnswerUI in a Python kernel. Run list_pyskills() to discover it, doc(answerui.skill) to read the guide, and doc(Btn) to inspect a component’s signature, declared variants, and CSS rules.

title: surfaces
text:
Card wraps content in a bordered section styled with the shared colour, spacing, and radius tokens. Badge renders an inline text label for a category, count, or status. Avatar renders a circular image or initials for a person or team.
from fasthtml.common import Article, Header, Footer, Small, to_xml
from answerui.layout import Grid
from answerui.controls import Btn
from answerui.demo import demo
from urllib.parse import quote

title: surfaces
text:
Card
Add the card attribute to any element for a --color-surface background, a 1px --color-border, --space padding, --radius corners, and a --raised shadow. [card] uses no bevels so cards do not look clickable. Card(...) returns a <section card> element and uses no JavaScript.
[card] sets no child layout. Pass stack=True for a vertical stack, or nest another layout inside the card.



Card
def Card(
    *c, **attrs
):
A bordered section with no prescribed layout


Inner padding comes from [card]. Add stack=True for spacing between children, and use a surrounding layout such as Grid or Stack to space cards apart.

Card.demo()


  
↻  




Composition
You can use any HTML structure inside a card without dedicated header, body, or footer constructors. Below, Grid arranges two cards side by side when the container is wide enough. The second card is an Article with card=True and stack=True directly, using stack=True on its Header and cluster=True on its Footer.

demo(Grid(
    _card_example(),
    Article(
        Header(H3('Field notes'), Small('Updated today'), stack=True, cls='gap-1'),
        P('Observations and ideas from the team, ready for the next meeting.'),
        Footer(Btn('Open project'), Btn('Archive', variant='secondary'), cluster=True),
        card=True, stack=True)))


  
↻  





Customisation
Overriding --radius or --space changes card corners and padding across a region. To restyle all cards without affecting other components, add a rule such as [card] { padding: var(--space1); } in @layer app. For a single card, pass utility classes such as cls='gap-2 p-2' (or inline style for custom values):

to_xml(Card(P('A compact note'), P('Another line'), stack=True, cls='gap-2 p-2'))

'<section card stack class="gap-2 p-2">\n  <p>A compact note</p>\n  <p>Another line</p>\n</section>\n'


You can combine card=True with any layout constructor, such as Grid(..., card=True), without adding a wrapper div. Plain article, section, and div elements without card have no card border or background.

title: surfaces
text:
Badge
Badge renders an inline <span> with a soft --v-3 background and --v2 text rather than the solid, raised fill used on buttons. Pass ui_tone (such as 'success', 'warning', 'danger', or 'info') to change its hue, or variant='secondary' for neutral --color-surface and --color-text styling with a 1px inset --color-border.



Badge
def Badge(
    *c, variant:NoneType=None, **attrs
):
A small text label, optionally coloured with ui_tone


Badges use em padding (.125em .5em) at --text-1 size so padding scales with the text. Put the meaning in the badge text and use colour only to reinforce it. [badge] is display-only, with no interaction or ARIA live-region role.

Badge.demo()


  
↻  



Badges have no outer margin. Below, Cluster places a badge beside the heading while Card(..., stack=True) spaces the rows apart. Pass counts as ordinary text children rather than CSS-generated content:

demo(Card(
    Cluster(H3('Field notes'), Badge('Shared'), cls='gap-2'),
    P('Observations and ideas from the team.'),
    Cluster(Span('Unread notes'), Badge(3, variant='secondary'), cls='gap-2'), stack=True))


  
↻

title: surfaces
text:
Avatar
Avatar takes a name and an optional image URL in src. With src, it renders an <img> with alt=name. Without src, it renders a <span role="img"> showing the first and last initials (or ? if name is empty) with aria-label set to name (or 'Unknown'). Both forms share the same circular frame controlled by --avatar-size (default 2.5rem), with initials sized to 40% of --avatar-size.



Avatar
def Avatar(
    name, src:NoneType=None, **attrs
):
A circular image or initials identifying a person or team



Avatar.demo()


  
↻  




def _picture(name): return f'https://api.dicebear.com/10.x/miniavs/svg?seed={quote(name)}&backgroundColor=ffe3ea'
demo(Cluster(Avatar('Ada Lovelace', src=_picture('Ada Lovelace'), aria_hidden='true'),
    Stack(Span('Ada Lovelace'), Small('Workspace owner'), cls='gap-1')))


  
↻  



To make an avatar clickable, place it as the only child of a Btn. The [btn]:has(> [avatar]:only-child) rule sets 1px padding, border-radius: var(--radius-full), --face: var(--color-surface), and --color-border on the button without overriding the avatar’s colours. When the button is disabled, the avatar has opacity: .5.

demo(Cluster(Btn(Avatar('Ada Lovelace')), Btn(Avatar('Grace Hopper', src=_picture('Grace Hopper'))),
    Btn(Avatar('Alan Turing', src=_picture('Alan Turing')), disabled=True)))


  
↻

title: demo
text:
demo renders ordinary FastHTML markup in an isolated document with the registry’s current styles, behaviors, and browser helpers from reg.hdrs(), matching a served app. Previews work in notebooks and generated docs without an asset server.
from answerui.registry import hypelt
from fastcore.test import *
from fasthtml.common import P, Details, Summary
from answerui.controls import Btn
from answerui.overlays import Dropdown

title: demo
text:
Rendering previews
Each preview document includes a stylesheet, behavior script, browser helpers, the icon spritesheet, and htmx. FastHTML’s def_hdrs returns the default app headers: charset and viewport meta tags, htmx 2, and FastHTML’s helper script. def_hdrs(htmx4=True) returns htmx 4 instead with an htmx-config meta tag setting metaCharacter to -, matching fast_app(htmx4=True). demo_html passes surreal=False to omit Surreal.
htmx comes before the behavior script in <head> because the behavior script registers with htmx. Both load before the page body, which includes spritesheet. Pass css to substitute a custom stylesheet without changing the registry, or registry to use another registry’s stylesheet, behavior script, and browser helpers instead of reg.
demo_html sets inline min-block-size: auto on body to override any full-viewport minimum height rule from the stylesheet. Without that override, an auto-resizing iframe would grow without end.
When FastHTML serves a page, it renames get, post, put, delete, patch, and link to hx-get, hx-post, hx-put, hx-delete, hx-patch, and href, turning each value into a URL. In a preview, demo_html renames those same attributes while keeping each path unchanged. Pass routes as a dict mapping 'METHOD path' keys such as 'GET /saved' to canned FastHTML responses. On a matching htmx:beforeRequest event, an inline script cancels the network request and swaps the canned markup into the target. It uses the element’s inherited hx-swap style, defaulting to innerHTML.



demo_html
def demo_html(
    *fts, # Markup to render
    registry:answerui.registry.Registry=Registry(21 rules, 21 elements), # Registry providing styles, behaviors, and browser helpers
    css:NoneType=None, # Custom CSS string; None uses the styles from registry.hdrs()
    htmx4:bool=False, # Use htmx 4 with FastHTML's config, as `fast_app(htmx4=True)` does, instead of htmx 2
    routes:NoneType=None, # Canned htmx responses as {'METHOD path': markup}
):
A standalone HTML document containing markup, CSS, behaviors, browser helpers, icon spritesheet, and FastHTML’s default headers


In notebooks, demo renders the preview inside an iframe. That isolates the preview from the host notebook’s CSS, such as Solveit’s styles, in both directions. The iframe’s srcdoc attribute holds the complete document from demo_html. Unless you pass height, an inline ResizeObserver script resizes the iframe to fit its content. Pass width to preview a narrow viewport. A replay button above the iframe reloads srcdoc to restart dynamic components such as a self-dismissing notice.
Because the iframe contains the full stylesheet and scripts, storing its HTML in every notebook output would bloat the file. demo returns a Preview object with two representations: the iframe as text/html for live display, and the markup alone as text/markdown for saved notebooks and language models.



demo
def demo(
    *fts, # Markup to render
    registry:answerui.registry.Registry=Registry(21 rules, 21 elements), # Registry providing styles, behaviors, and browser helpers
    css:NoneType=None, # Custom CSS string; None uses the styles from registry.hdrs()
    height:NoneType=None, # Fixed iframe height (e.g. '10rem') for top-layer content ResizeObserver cannot measure; None resizes to content
    width:NoneType=None, # Fixed iframe width, e.g. '24rem', to preview a narrow viewport; None fills the cell
    htmx4:bool=False, # Use htmx 4 with FastHTML's config, as `fast_app(htmx4=True)` does, instead of htmx 2
    routes:NoneType=None, # Canned htmx responses as {'METHOD path': markup}
):
Render markup in an isolated, replayable notebook preview





Preview
def Preview(
    fts, frame
):
A rendered preview: the iframe as HTML for live display, and the markup as Markdown for saved notebooks and models


A preview does not require a registered component. Here css='' replaces the registry’s stylesheet with an empty one, showing a native element exactly as the browser draws it:

demo(Details(Summary('More information'), P('This disclosure is a native details element.')), css='')


  
↻  



Let’s recreate the notice from the earlier notebooks with one hypelt call that registers its styles and behaviors together. Clicking its dismiss button removes the notice. With autodismiss set, the init handler removes the notice after that many milliseconds (4000 by default) once htmx loads it.

notice_css = r"""
display: block;
padding: .75rem 1rem;
background: #f4f4f6;
border: 1px solid #ccc;
border-radius: 8px;
"""
NoticeBox = hypelt('NoticeBox', css=notice_css, layer='components', on={
    ('& [dismiss]', 'click'): r"el.closest('notice-box').remove()",
    ('&[autodismiss]', 'init'): r"await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, +el.getAttribute('autodismiss') || 4000)); el.remove()"},
    doc='A dismissible notice.')

Click Dismiss, then click the replay button to restore the notice:

demo(NoticeBox('Changes saved. ', Button('Dismiss', type='button', dismiss=True)))


  
↻  



_repr_mimebundle_ returns both representations with {'nbdev': {'strip': ['text/html']}} metadata. nbdev-clean uses that metadata to strip the iframe HTML from saved notebook outputs and keep the Markdown:

bundle, meta = demo(NoticeBox('Changes saved.'))._repr_mimebundle_()
meta

{'nbdev': {'strip': ['text/html']}}


This notice disappears after four seconds:

demo(NoticeBox('This notice disappears after four seconds.', autodismiss=4000), height='4rem')


  
↻  



Here the Save button requests /saved. The canned response returns a NoticeBox and a Dropdown (a trigger and a panel). The routes script swaps the complete fragment into place as a served route would. Click Save, open Next action, then click the replay button to reset the preview.

demo(Button('Save', type='button', get='/saved', hx_swap='outerHTML'),
    routes={'GET /saved': (NoticeBox('Saved.'), Dropdown('Next action', Btn('Keep'), Btn('Remove')))})


  
↻  



Passing htmx4=True includes the same htmx 4 headers and FastHTML config as fast_app(htmx4=True). The behavior script runs init handlers through htmx.onLoad, which under that config listens for htmx 4’s htmx-after-process event on newly arrived content. The notice’s timer still starts:

demo(NoticeBox('This notice disappears after four seconds under htmx 4.', autodismiss=4000), htmx4=True, height='4rem')


  
↻  



Here we pass a candidate stylesheet via css that replaces the notice’s grey background with pale yellow. The registered behaviors still apply.

candidate_css = NoticeBox.rules['base'].compiled_css.replace('#f4f4f6', '#fff4cc')
demo(NoticeBox('Trying a warmer surface. ', Button('Dismiss', type='button', dismiss=True)), css=candidate_css)


  
↻  



To register an application override for all later previews and application pages, call NoticeBox.rule. It adds CSS to the app layer without changing the notice’s base definition or behaviors:

NoticeBox.rule('corners', 'border-radius: 1rem;', doc='Rounder notice corners.')
demo(NoticeBox('The current stylesheet includes the application override.'))


  
↻

title: demo
text:
Reusable examples
Use the example decorator to attach a no-argument markup function to a hyperelement as NoticeBox.example. Calling NoticeBox.demo() renders that markup with the hyperelement’s registry.
Attaching another example replaces the previous one. To show multiple variants, return them together from one function.



Hyperelement.demo
def demo(
    *, css:NoneType=None, # Custom CSS string; None uses the styles from registry.hdrs()
    height:NoneType=None, # Fixed iframe height (e.g. '10rem') for top-layer content ResizeObserver cannot measure; None resizes to content
    width:NoneType=None, # Fixed iframe width, e.g. '24rem', to preview a narrow viewport; None fills the cell
    htmx4:bool=False, # Use htmx 4 with FastHTML's config, as `fast_app(htmx4=True)` does, instead of htmx 2
    routes:NoneType=None, # Canned htmx responses as {'METHOD path': markup}
):
Render this hyperelement’s example with its registry’s current styles and behaviors





example
def example(
    h
):
Decorator that stores a no-argument markup function as h.example, for h.demo() to render



@example(NoticeBox)
def notice_example():
    return Div(NoticeBox('Changes saved. ', Button('Dismiss', type='button', dismiss=True)),
        NoticeBox('This notice stays visible.'), style='display:grid;gap:1rem')

The example itself is ordinary markup:

to_xml(NoticeBox.example())

'<div style="display:grid;gap:1rem">\n<notice-box>Changes saved. <button type="button" dismiss>Dismiss</button></notice-box><notice-box>This notice stays visible.</notice-box></div>\n'


NoticeBox.demo() renders it with the current styles and behaviors:

NoticeBox.demo()


  
↻  



NoticeBox.example() returns fresh FastHTML markup that can be inspected or reused in a larger composition. NoticeBox.demo() accepts demo’s options, such as height and css. Each call to NoticeBox.demo() builds a new document from the current example, styles, and behaviors. Clicking the replay button instead restarts interactions by reloading the existing srcdoc in the iframe without running Python.
Because each shipped component’s notebook exports its @example function, importing the component’s module attaches the example without rendering anything.
Registering corners again replaces the earlier rule in place. The next NoticeBox.demo() builds its document with the square corners:

NoticeBox.rule('corners', 'border-radius: 0;', doc='Square notice corners.')
NoticeBox.demo()


  
↻  



Calling hypelt again with the same name updates the existing NoticeBox in place, keeping its example:

NoticeBox = hypelt('NoticeBox', css=notice_css, layer='components', doc='A persistent notice.')
test_is(NoticeBox.example, notice_example)
NoticeBox.demo()


  
↻

title: hdrs
text:
For inline assets, pass reg.hdrs() and reg.ftrs() to FastHTML or fast_app. The headers include the shared foundation stylesheet, registered application rules, the delegated event script, and the shared browser helpers. The footer includes the fastlucide icon spritesheet. FastHTML renders the registry’s current rules on each response, including rules registered after app creation. To serve cached local asset URLs instead, call reg.serve(app). It mounts the asset routes and appends the headers and footers to app.
from fasthtml.common import *
from answerui.registry import reg, hypelt
from fastcore.test import *
from fastlucide.icons import Check
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

title: Palette
text:
Most design systems name colours by role (primary, secondary, surface, outline, muted, destructive) and hand-pick each swatch. Many roles need multiple shades (such as button fill, alert wash, and label), turning each role into a bundle of swatches. Every new state or theme (warning, dark mode) multiplies those bundles, leaving a hand-picked grid with no guarantee of completeness, consistency, or safe extension.
Instead, we build a generator that derives a complete colour family from a single hue. Each family is an ordinal ladder of prominence steps called rungs, where negative steps are less prominent and positive steps are more prominent. For example, step 0 is the solid fill, step +1 the hover state, and step -3 the page background. Attaching contrast or perceptual-separation targets to these rungs lets us compute every colour numerically rather than by eye.
AnswerUI uses two ladders. The vivid ladder defines accent colours (buttons, links, alert fills, and focus rings). The neutral ladder defines near-grey UI colours (page, surface, border, and text). By default the neutral ladder uses a cool blue hue (260), keeping surrounding text neutral when the accent hue changes. Set both --hue and --neutral-hue to the same value to tint a whole region together.
Computing rungs from stated targets lets us regenerate the palette whenever we change a contrast target, the number of rungs, or the neutral tint. The palette and generator have these requirements:



P1. Perceptual uniformity across hue: steps at the same prominence must look equally bright regardless of hue. A yellow solid and a blue solid at the same step should have the same visual weight, avoiding glowing buttons in some palettes and muted ones in others.
P2. Step distinctness: adjacent steps on each ladder must remain perceptually separable at every hue so users can distinguish neighbouring component states.
P3. Guaranteed contrast at every hue: contrast targets must hold across all hues, structured using WCAG 2 ratios.
P4. Hue interchangeability: any hue must produce a usable family without special cases or illegible, neon colours.
P5. Dual-theme support: light and dark themes must belong to the same family and independently meet every uniformity and contrast requirement.
P6. Context extensibility: adding a named context (danger, warning, success) requires only a hue value.





G1. Browser-native derivation: the browser computes colours from the hue at runtime without pre-computed colour tables or JavaScript.
G2. Gamut-aware: chroma at each step stays inside the sRGB gamut boundary for that lightness and hue, preventing silent browser clamping to unverified colours.
G3. Contrast-derived anchors: ladder steps with WCAG obligations (such as text on a primary button) are computed from contrast targets (P3) rather than chosen by eye. Steps without contrast obligations (backgrounds, interaction states) are spaced mechanically between anchored steps.
G4. Mechanical inputs: changing the number of steps requires adjusting minimal parameters while preserving aesthetic and functional consistency.
G5. Machine-verified: code checks gamut containment, contrast ratios, and adjacent-step distinctness, and verifies the generated CSS against those checks.

title: Palette
text:
Utilities
To build and verify the palette, we need utilities for OKLCH-to-sRGB conversion, WCAG relative luminance, and side-by-side colour swatches.

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, pandas as pd
from fasthtml.common import Div
from fastcore.test import *
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from nbdev.config import get_config
from textwrap import indent


plt.rcParams['figure.dpi'] = 75


OKLCH to sRGB
OKLCH represents a colour with three values: L for perceived lightness (0 to 1), C for chroma (colourfulness), and h for hue in degrees. It is the polar form of Oklab, published by Björn Ottosson in 2020 as a successor to CIELAB. Equal L gives equal perceived brightness across hue and chroma (P1). Equal steps in L produce uniform visual steps (P2). CSS supports oklch() natively.
Displaying or measuring a colour requires sRGB. Below we implement Ottosson’s conversion in both linear and gamma-encoded sRGB. WCAG contrast (P3) uses linear luminance, while hex swatches (P1, P2) use gamma-encoded sRGB.

M1 = np.array([[0.4122214708, 0.5363325363, 0.0514459929],
               [0.2119034982, 0.6806995451, 0.1073969566],
               [0.0883024619, 0.2817188376, 0.6299787005]])
M2 = np.array([[0.2104542553,  0.7936177850, -0.0040720468],
               [1.9779984951, -2.4285922050,  0.4505937099],
               [0.0259040371,  0.7827717662, -0.8086757660]])
M1i, M2i = np.linalg.inv(M1), np.linalg.inv(M2)

def oklch2lin(L, C, h):
    "Linear sRGB (unclamped) for oklch `L`, `C`, hue `h` in degrees"
    hr = np.deg2rad(h)
    lab = np.stack(np.broadcast_arrays(L, C*np.cos(hr), C*np.sin(hr)), axis=-1)
    return ((lab @ M2i.T)**3) @ M1i.T

def lin2srgb(lin): return np.where(lin <= .0031308, 12.92*lin, 1.055*np.abs(lin)**(1/2.4) - .055)
def rgb2hex(rgb): return '#%02x%02x%02x' % tuple(round(c*255) for c in np.clip(rgb, 0, 1))
def oklch2hex(L, C, h): return rgb2hex(lin2srgb(oklch2lin(L, C, h)))

We validate the conversion against two known colours: white (L=1, C=0) and sRGB pure red from MDN.

test_close(oklch2lin(1, 0, 0), [1, 1, 1], eps=1e-5)
test_close(lin2srgb(oklch2lin(.62796, .25768, 29.234)), [1, 0, 0], eps=1e-3)



Luminance and contrast
WCAG defines readability as the ratio of relative luminances between two colours:
[ ]
Here (Y) is the light a colour emits, weighted by human sensitivity to each primary according to the WCAG relative luminance formula:
[ Y = 0.2126,R + 0.7152,G + 0.0722,B ]
The targets are 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI components (P3).
Because standard sRGB values are gamma-encoded rather than linear light, we undo the gamma curve first and then apply the luminance weights to compute Y.

LUM = np.array([.2126, .7152, .0722])

def srgb2lin(rgb):
    "Undo sRGB gamma: the light actually emitted per channel, 0–1"
    rgb = np.asarray(rgb)
    return np.where(rgb <= .04045, rgb/12.92, ((rgb+.055)/1.055)**2.4)

def srgb2lum(rgb):
    "WCAG relative luminance of sRGB `rgb`, components 0–1"
    return srgb2lin(rgb) @ LUM

def oklch2lum(L, C, h):
    "WCAG relative luminance of an oklch colour"
    return oklch2lin(L, C, h) @ LUM

def hex2rgb(c): return np.array([int(c[i:i+2], 16)/255 for i in (1,3,5)])

def contrast(y1, y2):
    "WCAG contrast ratio between two relative luminances"
    lo, hi = np.minimum(y1, y2), np.maximum(y1, y2)
    return (hi + .05) / (lo + .05)

As a boundary check, WebAIM cites mid-grey #767676 on white as the lightest 8-bit grey that passes the 4.5:1 AA threshold. Its WCAG contrast ratio is 4.54:1.

test_close(contrast(srgb2lum(hex2rgb('#767676')), 1.), 4.54, eps=.01)

The luminance of #ff0000 (pure red) should match the luminance calculated from its oklch value:

test_close(oklch2lum(.62796, .25768, 29.234), srgb2lum(hex2rgb('#ff0000')), eps=1e-3)



Swatches
A row of colour chips with captions, for visual comparison of candidates.

def swatch(c, lbl=''):
    return Div(Div(style=f'background:{c};height:3rem;border-radius:4px'),
               Div(lbl, style='font-size:0.7rem;text-align:center'), style='flex:1')

def swatches(cs, lbls=None): return Div(*[swatch(c,l) for c,l in zip(cs, lbls or cs)], style='display:flex;gap:4px')

Motivating demo: a hue sweep at constant HSL “lightness” versus one at constant oklch L.

hs12 = range(0, 360, 30)
swatches([f'hsl({h} 100% 50%)' for h in hs12], [f'{h}°' for h in hs12])

0°30°60°90°120°150°180°210°240°270°300°330°


At HSL lightness 50%, perceived brightness varies sharply across hues. Yellow and cyan glow while blue recedes.

swatches([oklch2hex(.6, .15, h) for h in hs12], [f'{h}°' for h in hs12])

0°30°60°90°120°150°180°210°240°270°300°330°


The OKLCH row has uniform perceived brightness across hues, matching P1.

text:
Gamut Boundary
The sRGB gamut is small. At any lightness and hue, the maximum displayable chroma varies jaggedly with both. To avoid silent browser clamping (G2), we compute gamut membership directly.

def in_gamut(L, C, h, eps=1e-4):
    "True where oklch (`L`,`C`,`h`) lies inside sRGB: every linear channel in [0,1]"
    lin = oklch2lin(L, C, h)
    return ((lin > -eps) & (lin < 1+eps)).all(-1)


assert in_gamut(.62796, .25768, 29.234)         # pure red: on the boundary, inside
assert not in_gamut(.62796, .27,    29.234)     # a nudge more chroma: outside
assert in_gamut(1, 0, 0) and in_gamut(0, 0, 0)  # the achromatic poles

We find the maximum displayable chroma cmax(L, h) by bisection. The upper bracket 0.5 sits above sRGB’s global chroma maximum (about 0.32 near the blue primary).

def cmax(L, h, tol=1e-5):
    "Largest displayable chroma at lightness `L`, hue `h`"
    L, h = np.broadcast_arrays(np.asarray(L, float), np.asarray(h, float))
    lo, hi = np.zeros_like(L), np.full_like(L, .5)
    while (hi-lo).max() > tol:
        mid = (lo+hi)/2
        ok = in_gamut(L, mid, h)
        lo, hi = np.where(ok, mid, lo), np.where(ok, hi, mid)
    return lo


test_close(cmax(.62796, 29.234), .25768, eps=1e-3)
assert cmax(1, 180) < 1e-3

Plot cmax for all hues across six lightness slices (line colours are arbitrary):

hs = np.arange(360)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
for L in (.95, .85, .70, .55, .40, .25): ax.plot(hs, cmax(L, hs), label=f'L={L}')
for h, c in [(110, 'gold'), (265, 'steelblue')]: ax.axvline(h, ls=':', lw=1.5, color=c)
ax.set(xlabel='hue (deg)', ylabel='Cmax', title='sRGB gamut boundary: max chroma by hue, per lightness slice')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1)); ax.grid(True, alpha=.3)








The boundary curve has sharp cusps near the sRGB primaries and secondaries, with a shape that varies by lightness. Yellow (110°, gold dotted line) reaches high chroma at high L and low chroma at low L, while blue (265°, blue dotted line) does the opposite.

for L in (.85, .55, .25):
    print(f'L={L}')
    display(swatches([oklch2hex(L, c, h) for c,h in zip(cmax(L, hs12), hs12)], [f'{h}°' for h in hs12]))

L=0.55
L=0.25

Vivid chroma
The boundary swatches show that maximum chroma is a physical limit rather than an aesthetic target. At medium lightness all hues look balanced. At high lightness (used for background washes) some hues look garish, while at low lightness blue stands out more than every other hue.
Capping every hue to the narrowest gamut eliminates the garish washes, at the cost of muddy colours at medium lightness. Instead, we use a chroma ceiling that tapers near black and white and peaks at medium lightness.
A simple candidate is a quadratic in lightness: zero at L=0 and L=1, peaking at L=0.5.

def ctarget(L, peak=.2):
    "Chroma ceiling: zero at the poles, `peak` at L=.5"
    return peak * 4*L*(1-L)

def palette_c(L, h, peak=.2):
    return np.minimum(ctarget(L, peak), cmax(L, h))


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

for L in (.95, .85, .70, .55, .40, .25):
    line, = ax.plot(hs, palette_c(L, hs), label=f'L={L}')
    clr = line.get_color()
    ax.plot(hs, cmax(L, hs), color=clr, alpha=.18)
    ax.axhline(ctarget(L), color=clr, ls=':', alpha=.5)

ax.set(
    xlabel='hue (deg)', ylabel='chroma',
    title='Palette chroma: aesthetic target constrained by sRGB gamut')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1))
ax.grid(True, alpha=.3)









for L in (.95, .85, .70, .55, .40, .25):
    display(swatches(
        [oklch2hex(L, palette_c(L, h), h) for h in hs12],
        [f'{h}°' for h in hs12]))

The quadratic lowers chroma at high lightness while the sRGB gamut caps most dark colours, though the lightest rows still look slightly pastel. Adding a shape exponent narrows the curve near the poles without changing the peak at L=0.5.

def ctarget(L, peak=.2, shape=1.):
    "Chroma ceiling: zero at the poles, `peak` at L=.5; `shape` above 1 lowers it everywhere else"
    return peak * (4*L*(1-L))**shape


Ls = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
for shape in (.7, 1, 1.5):
    plt.plot(Ls, ctarget(Ls, shape=shape), label=f'{shape=}')
plt.xlabel('lightness'); plt.ylabel('target chroma')
plt.legend(); plt.grid(alpha=.3)

    return np.minimum(ctarget(L, peak, shape), cmax(L, h))

Setting shape=1.5 trims chroma in the pale and dark rows without altering the mid-lightness solids. The L=.95 row now looks like gently tinted surfaces rather than pastel accents. We adopt peak=.2 and shape=1.5.


Neutral chroma
Vivid rungs need strong colour without looking garish. Neutral rungs should remain neutral while keeping enough of the neutral hue to tint surfaces and text.
Oklab uses three axes: perceived lightness (L), green-to-red (a), and blue-to-yellow (b). OKLCH is its polar form with chroma (C) and hue (h) in place of (a) and (b).
Oklab defines a perceptual colour-difference metric (E_{}) for how different two colours look:
[ E_{} = ]
Between an achromatic colour ((L, 0, h)) and a chromatic colour at the same lightness and hue, (L = 0) and the combined difference in (a) and (b) equals (C):
[ E_{} = C ]
Chroma is therefore the perceptual distance from grey in Oklab units. CSS Color 4 (§14.2.1) defines one just-noticeable difference (JND) as (E_{} = 0.02). A neutral colour with (C = 0.02) is barely distinguishable from pure grey. See Binary Search Gamut Mapping.

JND = .02
L = .7
swatches([oklch2hex(L, np.minimum(JND, cmax(L, h)), h) for h in hs12], [f'{h}°' for h in hs12])

text:
Ladder Design
Here we choose the steps for each ladder and assign their targets. Next we solve for the lightness of each step from those targets.

Parameters
We initialise a params dict to hold the tunable aesthetic parameters:

params = dict(
    vivid_peak=.2, vivid_shape=1.5,  # aesthetic chroma ceiling
    neutral_tint=1,                  # neutral tint, in JNDs from grey
)

def vivid_ceil(L): return ctarget(L, params['vivid_peak'], params['vivid_shape'])
def neutral_ceil(L): return params['neutral_tint']*JND
def capped(ceil, L, h): return np.minimum(ceil(L), cmax(L, h))



Base/page colour
The least-prominent rung (n-3) sets the default page background. App backgrounds sit near white or black rather than at pure extremes. Choosing pole_contrast = 1.02 keeps the page background close enough to white or black while still allowing a visible tint.

params['pole_contrast'] = 1.02

For pure grey (C=0) in OKLCH, relative luminance is (Y = L^3). Solving the WCAG contrast formula against white ((Y = 1)) and black ((Y = 0)) gives:

base = dict(
    light=np.cbrt(1.05/params['pole_contrast'] - .05),
    dark=np.cbrt(.05*(params['pole_contrast'] - 1)))
base

{'light': np.float64(0.993089611430119),
 'dark': np.float64(0.10000000000000002)}


With one JND of tint in the neutral ladder, luminance and contrast vary slightly with hue. We find the hue that yields the lowest contrast against the pole.

hgrid = np.arange(360)

def worst_pole_contrast(L, mode):
    "Lowest contrast between the neutral base at lightness `L` and its pole (white in light `mode`, black in dark), and the hue where it occurs"
    pole = 1 if mode == 'light' else 0
    ys = oklch2lum(L, capped(neutral_ceil, L, hgrid), hgrid)
    cs = contrast(ys, pole)
    i = np.argmin(cs)
    return cs[i], hgrid[i]

def solve_L(f, target, a=0, b=1):
    "Lightness between `a` and `b` where scalar function `f(L)` equals `target`"
    return brentq(lambda L: f(L) - target, *sorted((a, b)))

A single pole_contrast is asymmetric in JND units: about 0.5 JND from white, but 5 JNDs from black. The +0.05 flare term in the WCAG contrast formula models ambient light scattering, which masks small luminance steps near black far more than near white. Under normal viewing, using the same contrast ratio makes both page backgrounds look equally close to their poles despite the different JND distances.


Ladder jobs
Radix Colors defines a twelve-step scale covering app and subtle backgrounds (1-2), component backgrounds and hover/selected states (3-5), borders and focus rings (6-8), solid fills (9-10), and text (11-12).
AnswerUI splits those twelve roles across two six-step signed ladders. The neutral ladder (n-3 through n2) provides page, surface, border, and ordinary text colours. The vivid ladder (v-3 through v2) provides washes, rings, solid fills, and accent text.
Unlike Radix’s hand-tuned swatches, we assign each role to a rung as a job with a measurable target.
We measure targets with two units. Contrast measures text legibility from luminance alone. Distinguishing a raised surface or wash from the page depends on perceptible difference (including tint) rather than legibility. For those rungs we require sep = 2 JNDs in (E_{}). A wash only 1 JND from a card is barely visible.

params['sep'] = 2


def job(desc, c=None, bg='n-3', d=None):
    "A rung use: contrast `c` (or a light/dark pair) or ΔEOK `d`, measured against `bg`"
    return dict(desc=desc, c=c, bg=bg, d=d)

def contrast_target(job, mode):
    c = job['c']
    return c[mode == 'dark'] if isinstance(c, tuple) else c

def ladder(ceil, rungs):
    "A family of rungs sharing the aesthetic ceiling `ceil(L)`: each rung name mapped to its jobs and ceiling"
    return {nm: dict(jobs=js if isinstance(js, tuple) else (js,), ceil=ceil) for nm, js in rungs.items()}

The neutral ladder uses near-zero chroma (neutral_ceil). Its first rung (n-3) is the page background derived from pole_contrast. Every other rung is placed relative to it.

    'n-3': job('base: the lightness extreme (the default page)'),
    'n-2': job('raised surface: cards, inputs', d=params['sep']),
    'n-1': job('hairline borders, separators'),
    'n':   job('disabled text and controls'),
    'n1':  job('muted and placeholder text', c=4.5, bg='n-2'),
    'n2':  (job('body text', c=(7, 10)), job('body text on surface', c=(7, 10), bg='n-2')),
})

    'v-2': job('wash hover, selected'),

Ladder Optimisation
With the bases fixed, we can generalize the same calculation to any pair of ladder rungs.

def worst_contrast(L1, C1, L2, C2):
    "Lowest contrast between two rungs over every pair of context hues, one hue for each rung"
    y1, y2 = oklch2lum(L1, C1, hgrid), oklch2lum(L2, C2, hgrid)
    return contrast(y1[:,None], y2[None,:]).min()

def worst_sep(L1, C1, L2, C2):
    "Lowest same-hue ΔEOK between two rungs, in JNDs"
    return np.sqrt((L1-L2)**2 + (C1-C2)**2).min()/JND

Before solving the contrast-pinned rungs, we check that contrast changes monotonically as vivid lightness moves away from the base.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for mode, baseL in base.items():

    cs = [worst_contrast(L, capped(vivid_ceil, L, hgrid), baseL, capped(neutral_ceil, baseL, hgrid)) for L in Ls]
    ax.plot(Ls, cs, label=mode)

Because worst-hue contrast crosses each target once as lightness moves away from the base, we can solve each rung’s lightness with solve_L. The light and dark curves have different shapes, showing that dark-mode lightnesses cannot be obtained by inverting light mode and must be solved separately.

Rungs with targets
To place a rung, we search outward from its background for the first lightness at which every job passes. For example, a c=4.5 job passes once its worst-hue contrast against its background reaches 4.5.
Each candidate rung is evaluated as an (L, C) pair: the trial lightness and the family chroma ceiling capped by the sRGB gamut at that lightness.

def py_chroma(nm, L, h=hgrid):
    "Derived chroma of rung `nm` at lightness `L`: its family ceiling capped by the gamut"
    return capped(rungs[nm]['ceil'], L, h)

def LC(nm, L, chroma=py_chroma):
    "Rung `nm` at lightness `L`, as the (L, C) pair that `worst_contrast` and `worst_sep` take"
    return L, chroma(nm, L)

We’ll pad targets by a small margin to account for 8-bit rounding.

A rung can have multiple jobs. Dividing each measurement by its target puts all jobs on a common scale where 1 means the job passes. A rung passes when its lowest job ratio reaches 1. Starting from the most prominent background, a single root search finds the lightness where that minimum ratio equals margin. For example, the wash v-3 must stay distinct from both n-3 (page) and n-2 (surface):

def score(L): return min(
    worst_sep(*LC('v-3', L), *LC('n-3', lv['n-3'])) / params['sep'],
    worst_sep(*LC('v-3', L), *LC('n-2', lv['n-2'])) / params['sep'])

We now generalise this to any rung. Passing a chroma function into the solver lets us re-run the same optimisation against the chroma computed by CSS oklch().

def job_ratio(j, lc, bg, mode):
    "Worst-case measurement of job `j` divided by its target: at least 1 passes"
    if c := contrast_target(j, mode): return worst_contrast(*lc, *bg) / c
    return worst_sep(*lc, *bg) / j['d']

def solve_jobs(mode, nm, levels, chroma=py_chroma):
    "First lightness for `nm`, moving outward from its most prominent background, at which every targeted job passes, measured with `chroma`"
    jobs = [j for j in rungs[nm]['jobs'] if j['c'] or j['d']]
    bgs = {j['bg']: LC(j['bg'], levels[j['bg']], chroma) for j in jobs}
    start = (min if mode == 'light' else max)(L for L, _ in bgs.values())
    return solve_L(lambda L: min(job_ratio(j, LC(nm, L, chroma), bgs[j['bg']], mode) for j in jobs),
                   params['margin'], start, 0 if mode == 'light' else 1)

def interp_unpinned(ladder, mode, levels, chroma=py_chroma):
    "Fill each run of unpinned rungs with log-spaced base contrasts between its placed neighbours"
    def cb(nm, L): return worst_contrast(*LC(nm, L, chroma), *LC('n-3', levels['n-3'], chroma))
    nms, edge = list(ladder), 0 if mode == 'light' else 1
    pins = [i for i, nm in enumerate(nms) if nm in levels]
    for a, b in zip(pins, pins[1:]):
        ts = np.geomspace(cb(nms[a], levels[nms[a]]), cb(nms[b], levels[nms[b]]), b-a+1)
        for nm, t in zip(nms[a+1:b], ts[1:-1]): levels[nm] = solve_L(lambda L: cb(nm, L), t, levels['n-3'], edge)

Because every target references an earlier rung, solving pinned rungs in declaration order resolves each background before it is needed. Interpolation then fills the unpinned rungs.

def fit_ladders(mode, chroma=py_chroma):
    "Lightness of every rung in `mode`: the base, then pinned rungs in declaration order, then the rest by interpolation"
    levels = {'n-3': solve_L(lambda L: worst_pole_contrast(L, mode)[0], params['pole_contrast'])}
    for nm, r in rungs.items():
        if any(j['c'] or j['d'] for j in r['jobs']): levels[nm] = solve_jobs(mode, nm, levels, chroma)
    for lad in (neutral, vivid): interp_unpinned(lad, mode, levels, chroma)
    return {nm: levels[nm] for nm in rungs}

In the stylesheet each rung is a light-dark() pair. The browser uses --hue for the vivid ladder and --neutral-hue for the neutral ladder. Lightness is the constant solved above, while chroma is the smaller of the rung’s aesthetic ceiling and the sRGB gamut boundary at that lightness. We approximate that hue-dependent chroma with a CSS expression and re-verify every job against the emitted CSS values.

Boundary approximation
When a rung’s ceiling stays inside sRGB at every hue, the CSS can use that ceiling as a constant. Only rungs whose ceiling crosses the gamut boundary at some hue need a hue-dependent approximation. Below we compute the fraction of hues constrained by the gamut boundary for each rung:

Because the capped gamut boundary is periodic in hue and CSS supports trigonometric functions, we can approximate it with a truncated Fourier series in --hue.
The approximation must never exceed the sRGB boundary (G2). Ordinary least squares penalises overshoot and undershoot equally. We iteratively double the weight on overshooting hues until the curve stays below the target everywhere, then subtract any remaining positive residual from the constant term.

def harmonics(h, K):
    "Fourier design matrix over hues `h` in degrees: 1, cos kh, sin kh for k=1..K"
    hr = np.deg2rad(h)[:,None]*np.arange(1, K+1)
    return np.concatenate([np.ones((len(h),1)), np.cos(hr), np.sin(hr)], axis=1)

def fit_below(g, K, iters=40):
    "Coefficients of a `K`-harmonic fit that approaches `g` from below"
    X, w = harmonics(hgrid, K), np.ones_like(g)
    for _ in range(iters):
        sw = np.sqrt(w)[:,None]
        co = np.linalg.lstsq(X*sw, g*sw[:,0], rcond=None)[0]
        over = X@co > g
        if not over.any(): break
        w[over] *= 2
    co[0] -= max(0, (X@co - g).max())
    return co

def fit_rung(nm, mode, K):
    "Coefficients approximating rung `nm`'s derived chroma from below"
    return fit_below(rung_c(nm, mode), K)

    ax.set(xlabel='hue (deg)', ylabel='chroma', title=f'{m} {nm}: fitting the capped chroma from below')
    ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=.3)

Assembly
Every rung now has a solved lightness and a CSS-computable chroma function to pack into the stylesheet.
Writing the Fourier series in amplitude-phase form halves the term count, turning a cos(kh) + b sin(kh) into R cos(kh - φ). We round each coefficient and drop terms with amplitude below 1e-5. Subtracting dropped amplitudes and rounding overshoot from the constant term keeps the series below the target everywhere.

def floor5(x):
    "Round down to 5 decimals, keeping one-sided approximations one-sided"
    return float(np.floor(x*1e5)/1e5)

def eval_terms(c0, terms, h):
    "The chroma series `c0 + Σ R cos(kh - φ)` at hues `h`"
    hr = np.deg2rad(np.asarray(h, float))
    return c0 + sum((R*np.cos(k*hr - np.deg2rad(phi)) for k, R, phi in terms), np.zeros_like(hr))

def round_fit(co, g):
    "Amplitude-phase form of `co`, rounded and pruned, kept one-sided under target `g`"
    K = (len(co)-1)//2
    c0, terms = co[0], []
    for k in range(1, K+1):
        R = np.hypot(co[k], co[K+k])
        if R < 1e-5: c0 -= R; continue
        terms.append((k, round(float(R), 5), round(float(np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(co[K+k], co[k]))) % 360, 2)))
    c0 -= max(0, (eval_terms(c0, terms, hgrid) - g).max())
    return floor5(c0), terms

Collect the rounded lightness, ceiling, and harmonic terms for each rung:

ship = {}
for m in levels:
    for nm, L in levels[m].items():
        s = dict(L=round(L, 4), T=floor5(ceiling(nm, m)))
        if (m, nm) in fits: s['c0'], s['terms'] = round_fit(fits[(m, nm)], py_chroma(nm, s['L']))
        else: s['c0'], s['terms'] = s['T'], []
        ship[(m, nm)] = s

def css_chroma(nm, mode, h=hgrid):
    "Chroma the emitted CSS computes for rung `nm`: the rounded series, clamped to the rounded ceiling"
    s = ship[(mode, nm)]
    return np.clip(eval_terms(s['c0'], s['terms'], np.atleast_1d(h)), 0, s['T'])

For an unconstrained rung, chroma_expr emits a single constant. For a gamut-constrained rung, it emits clamp(0, series, ceiling) using --neutral-hue or --hue in each cosine term. ladder_css formats every rung as a light-dark() custom property with its job descriptions in a trailing comment.

def chroma_expr(s, hue):
    "CSS for the chroma: a constant, or the clamped series derived from `hue`"
    if not s['terms']: return f"{s['T']}"
    series = f"{s['c0']}" + ''.join(f" + {R}*cos(({k}*{hue} - {phi})*1deg)" for k, R, phi in s['terms'])
    return f"clamp(0, {series}, {s['T']})"

def color_css(nm, mode):
    "The rung's CSS colour, derived from its own ladder's hue"
    s = ship[(mode, nm)]
    hue = 'var(--neutral-hue)' if nm in neutral else 'var(--hue)'
    return f"oklch({s['L']} {chroma_expr(s, hue)} {hue})"

def ladder_css():
    "Every rung as a light-dark pair, with its jobs in the trailing comment"
    def tok(nm): return f"--{nm}: light-dark({color_css(nm, 'light')}, {color_css(nm, 'dark')});"
    def jobs(nm): return '; '.join(j['desc'] for j in rungs[nm]['jobs'])
    return '\n'.join(f"{tok(nm)} /* {jobs(nm)} */" for nm in rungs) + '\n'

title: navigation
text:
Navbar
By default, NavBar uses the page background (--color-background) with a bottom hairline border (--color-border) and places the brand, navigation, and end actions on one row. Links appear as plain text. Mark the current link with aria_current='page' to highlight it with the accent wash (--v-3 background and --v2 text, or --tint on a vivid bar).
Pass align='center' to centre <nav> between the brand and end actions, or align='end' to align <nav> beside end (the default align='start' places links right after the brand). Pass sticky=True to keep the bar pinned to the top while scrolling. Pass vivid=True for an accent surface (--color-accent with --color-on-accent text), and theme='light' or theme='dark' to override the inherited colour scheme (ui-theme).
When collapse=True and navigation items are passed, NavBar adds a disclosure button. The shared mountNavbar controller measures the actual row width instead of using a fixed viewport breakpoint, and hides <nav> behind that button whenever the row overflows. Opening the disclosure shows the same <nav> in normal flow below the bar without duplicating its content. Clicking a link, clicking outside the bar, or pressing Escape closes the menu. Pressing Escape returns focus to the disclosure button. Content passed as end stays visible in the bar.

Tables
When you pass table=True to Table, thead th and tfoot th are semibold (--weight1), with horizontal borders under the header and between body and footer rows. Any caption appears below the table in muted --text-1 text. Add num=True to a Th or Td to align it to the end with tabular digits (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums). DataTable wraps Table(*c, table=True) in a Div with table_frame=True ([table-frame]). That container has a border, a --raised shadow, overflow-x: auto, and contain: inline-size. Because of contain: inline-size, a wide table scrolls inside the frame rather than widening the page or its containing card. Inside [table-frame], thead th has a --color-surface background and cells stay on one line (white-space: nowrap). Keyword attributes passed to DataTable apply to the outer Div. Alert
Alert renders a message and optional supporting content on a tinted accent surface ([alert]). Pass ui_tone ('warning', 'danger', 'success', or 'info') to choose a severity hue. With dismissible=True, clicking the close button removes the alert through the delegated click listener in browser.js. Because that listener is attached to document, alerts inserted later by htmx are dismissible without extra wiring.



Alert
def Alert(
    *c, dismissible:bool=False, **attrs
):
An in-page message with optional dismissal


Severity colour and screen-reader announcements are separate choices. Alert adds no role by default because a persistent warning need not interrupt a screen-reader user. For polite feedback, place an empty role="status" region in the page first, then insert or update the message inside it. Reserve role="alert" for urgent messages. Screen readers do not reliably announce a message when a single swap creates the live region with the message already inside it. See ARIA live regions.

Alert.demo()


  
↻  



Alerts have no auto-dismiss timer because important information must stay visible until the user reads or closes it.

title: status
text:
Toast
Place an empty Toaster() in the page before delivering messages to it. Toaster renders a polite live region (role="status", aria-live="polite") with popover="manual". When a [toaster] mounts, browser.js calls showPopover(). Because it is a manual popover, the browser draws it above ordinary page content and leaves it open when the user clicks outside or presses Escape. Pass toaster_position ('top-start', 'bottom-start', or 'bottom-end') to move it from the default top-end corner. A modal dialog opened later sits above the toaster. Put feedback needed during a modal interaction inside that dialog.
By default, Toast sets --toast-duration: 5000ms (controlled by life) for the ui-toast-lifetime CSS animation. While the pointer hovers over a toast or keyboard focus is inside it, CSS pauses that animation (animation-play-state: paused). When animationend fires for ui-toast-lifetime, browser.js removes the toast. Passing life=None omits --toast-duration to keep the toast visible until the user dismisses it. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, --motion drops to 0ms while --toast-duration stays unchanged.



Toaster
def Toaster(
    *c, **attrs
):
The page’s polite live region for toast deliveries





Toast
def Toast(
    *c, life:int=5000, dismissible:bool=True, oob:bool=False, **attrs
):
A brief message for the toast region


Deliver a toast inside an out-of-band wrapper with Div(Toast('Saved'), hx_swap_oob='beforeend:[toaster]') or Toast('Saved', oob=True). During a beforeend swap, htmx discards the outer element and appends its children. Wrapping the toast keeps the [toast] element, its attributes, and its dismiss button intact. Putting hx_swap_oob directly on Toast would make htmx discard the [toast] element and append only its inner nodes. See out-of-band swaps.
The example below stores the out-of-band wrapper in a template element whose HTML the button’s hx-on:click handler passes to htmx.swap. This demonstrates delivery without a server or a registered behavior. In an app, return the wrapper directly from a route with no inline script. Click the button to deliver both messages, then try hovering or focusing the timed toast.

Toast.demo(height='14rem')


  
↻  




Queued toasts
A redirect response contains no HTML for a toast. An htmx route returns a partial fragment rather than a full page with a Toaster. In both cases, call add_toast(sess, msg, life=5000, **attrs) to queue the message in the session under toasts_key ('aui_toasts'), passing severity as an attribute such as ui_tone='success'.
On a full-page route, render queued toasts inside Toaster(*pop_toasts(sess)). On a fragment route, include toasts_oob(sess) in the response for htmx to swap into the existing [toaster]. Call setup_toasts(app) to register toast_after on app.after and inject toasts_oob(sess) automatically on every markup or empty response. toast_after does nothing when the queue is empty, as happens after a full-page route calls pop_toasts(sess).

The toasts queued in session sess, in an out-of-band wrapper for delivery beside a fragment, clearing the queue; None when nothing is queued

The toasts queued in session sess, as Toasts, clearing the queue

Deliver queued toasts out of band with every markup or empty response of app

title: registry
text:
AnswerUI provides built-in components through its shared stylesheet and JavaScript assets. Python constructors render their marked HTML. This registry holds application CSS and event handlers, attaches custom rules to constructors, and assembles those additions for each page. Built-in CSS remains in the shared assets instead of being copied into registry entries.
from fasthtml.common import Label, Input, Button, to_xml
from fastcore.test import *

title: registry
text:
Rules
Both styling and behavior pair a CSS selector with an action: CSS declarations for styling, or an event name and JavaScript handler for behavior. A Rule stores both CSS text and behavior records under a cascade layer because each page loads one combined stylesheet and one combined script.
The layer list is fixed and ordered. For normal declarations, each layer overrides earlier layers regardless of specificity. You can restyle a built-in component from the app layer without changing its definition. Component and base CSS do not use !important because !important reverses cascade-layer order (only the hidden-state classes in utilities use it).
Behaviors are passed as a dict from (selector, event) keys to JavaScript handler bodies. Each handler runs with el bound to the matched element and e to the event. For an event that doesn’t bubble, such as toggle, add a truthy third item to the key to attach the handler in the capture phase. When a rule has a root selector sel, _behaviors replaces each & in its behavior selectors with :is(sel) (raising ValueError if sel is missing).
A rule’s key is a name, or owner.name when the rule belongs to a hyperelement. Rule checks the layer, expands the behaviors, and derives owner and name from the key. For a variant rule, the variant attribute is stored in variant:



Rule
def Rule(
    key, # Registry key: a name, or `owner.name` for a hyperelement's rule
    css:str='', # Complete CSS, or a no-argument function returning it
    *, on:NoneType=None, # Mapping of (selector, event[, capture]) to JavaScript handler bodies
    sel:NoneType=None, # Root selector substituted for `&` in behaviors
    layer:str='app', # One of LAYERS
    doc:str='', # Description of the rule
    variant:NoneType=None, # Attribute selecting a declared variant
):
A named CSS and behavior definition in a cascade layer


Registry.rule takes CSS first and an optional name second. Without a name, it hashes the CSS, selector, expanded behaviors and layer into a deterministic key. Identical registrations share one entry, including behavior-only rules. Pass an explicit name when css is callable, or when later edits should replace the previous rule rather than add another. A component’s rule uses owner.name as its key.
Rules are stored in Registry.rules. Registering an existing key updates that Rule object in place, preserving both existing references and its position in the stylesheet. Registering or removing a rule increments version, which Registry.assets checks before rebuilding the stylesheet and script. Each entry of layers is a live RuleView of the rules in that layer:



Registry
def Registry():
Named rules and hyperelements, from which a page’s stylesheet and script are built





RuleView
def RuleView(
    registry, *, layer:NoneType=None, owner:NoneType=None
):
A live, read-only view of one layer or one hyperelement’s rules


The simplest rule is bare CSS with no constructor, such as a centered page column. Its layer defaults to app. Registering the same name again returns the existing entry:

page_css = 'main { max-width: 65ch; margin-inline: auto; padding: 1rem; }'
page_rule = reg.rule(page_css, 'app-page', doc='A centered single-column page.')
test_eq(page_rule.css, page_css)
test_is(reg.rule(page_css, 'app-page', doc='A centered single-column page.'), page_rule)

A standalone behavior works the same way. Here we add a select-all attribute that selects an input’s text on focus. Passing sel='input[select-all]' sets the root selector that & expands to in the handler key. The rule stores the expanded behavior record:

select_all = reg.rule(name='select-all', sel='input[select-all]', on={('&', 'focusin'): r"el.select()"},
    doc='Select the input text when it receives focus.')

Building the stylesheet
build_css starts with the shared styles.css, whose opening @layer statement declares the layer order. Registered rules follow as one @layer block per layer in registration order, each preceded by a comment naming its key. Application rules default to app, after the built-in components layer. For CSS that depends on later registrations, pass a zero-argument callable that build_css evaluates during assembly.



Registry.build_css
def build_css():
The shared foundation followed by registered CSS in cascade-layer order

title: registry
text:
Hyperelements
A component pairs a constructor (a standard FastTag or a Python function combining multiple tags) with registered rules. Calling a Hyperelement invokes that constructor. Its sel attribute holds the root selector. Its rules attribute is a live RuleView of the component’s rules:



Hyperelement
def Hyperelement(
    registry, name, fn, sel, doc:str='', generated:bool=False
):
A callable constructor linked to its registered rules and behaviors


Use Hyperelement.rule to add CSS nested under the root selector, or Hyperelement.variant to add an attribute variant nested under :is(sel)[name]. Both register their rule with the hyperelement as its owner. Calling variant also stores the attribute name on the rule (base is reserved for the constructor’s own rule):



Hyperelement.variant
def variant(
    name, # Attribute selecting the variant; also its local rule name
    css:str='', # CSS declarations and nested rules, scoped to the variant
    *, on:NoneType=None, # Mapping of (selector, event[, capture]) to handler bodies; `&` is the variant selector
    layer:str='app', # One of LAYERS
    doc:str='', # Description shown with the variant
):
Declare an attribute variant without changing the constructor





Hyperelement.rule
def rule(
    name, # Local rule name; registering it again replaces that rule
    css:str='', # CSS declarations and nested rules, scoped to the root selector
    *, on:NoneType=None, # Mapping of (selector, event[, capture]) to handler bodies; `&` is the root selector
    layer:str='app', # One of LAYERS
    doc:str='', # Description of the customization
):
Register CSS and behaviors scoped to this hyperelement


hypelt registers a component from a FastHTML tag name or a handwritten constructor and nests css under its root selector as the base rule, just like Hyperelement.rule. Write declarations for the root, nested selectors for children, and & for states or pseudo-elements on the root. Pass a callable with no parameters when css depends on later registrations. Put global rules such as @keyframes in reg.rule, which accepts complete CSS without wrapping and uses its sel parameter for behaviors only. The module-level hypelt is bound to reg:



Registry.hypelt
def hypelt(
    name:NoneType=None, # FastHTML tag name or a constructor; omit to use as a decorator
    *, sel:NoneType=None, # Root selector; required for a handwritten constructor
    css:str='', # CSS declarations and nested rules, or a no-argument function returning them
    on:NoneType=None, # Mapping of (selector, event[, capture]) to JavaScript handler bodies
    layer:str='app', # One of LAYERS; built-ins use components, layout, or base
    doc:NoneType=None, # Description; defaults to a handwritten constructor's docstring
):
Register a constructor and its base rule, returning a callable hyperelement


As an example component, let’s build a dismissible notice box with a close button. Because HTML has no built-in notice element, we use the custom tag notice-box. Clicking any child with the dismiss attribute removes the notice:

notice_css = r"""
display: block;
padding: .75rem 1rem;
background: #f4f4f6;
border: 1px solid #ccc;
border-radius: 8px;
"""
NoticeBox = hypelt('NoticeBox', css=notice_css, on={('& [dismiss]', 'click'): r"el.closest('notice-box').remove()"},
    layer='components', doc='A dismissible notice.')
to_xml(NoticeBox('Changes saved.', Button('Dismiss', dismiss=True)))

'<notice-box>Changes saved.<button dismiss>Dismiss</button></notice-box>'


For a string name such as 'NoticeBox', hypelt looks up the constructor on fasthtml.components and calls it with no arguments to get the root selector (notice-box). NoticeBox.rules and reg.rules hold the same Rule object:

test_eq(NoticeBox().tag, NoticeBox.sel)
assert NoticeBox.rules['base'] is reg.rules['NoticeBox.base']
assert NoticeBox.rules['base'].compiled_css.startswith('notice-box {')
NoticeBox

NoticeBox(*children, **attrs)
A dismissible notice.
Root selector: notice-box.
Rules: - base (components)


The second case is a handwritten constructor, such as a labelled field that wraps an input inside its label to associate them without an id. Because Field requires a label argument, hypelt can’t call it with no arguments to infer a root selector. Instead we mark the label with a field attribute and pass sel='label[field]' using the decorator form:

field_css = r"""
display: grid;
gap: .5rem;
"""

@hypelt(sel='label[field]', css=field_css)
def Field(label, **attrs):
    "A labelled input"
    return Label(label, Input(**attrs), field=True)

to_xml(Field('Email', name='email', type='email'))

'<label field>Email  <input name="email" type="email">\n</label>'

title: registry
text:
Customization
There are two ways to change a component’s styling or behavior. To override a component without altering its base rule, register separate rules in the app layer. To redefine it, call hypelt again with the same name to replace its constructor and base rule in place.

Overrides
Say a developer wants rounder notices in their application. NoticeBox.rule registers a named rule in the app layer by default, where it overrides the component’s CSS in the components layer:

NoticeBox.rule('corners', 'border-radius: 1rem;', doc='Rounder notices in this application.')

NoticeBox.corners [app] notice-box: Rounder notices in this application.


To select a style with an attribute, declare it with variant. Its description then appears in the hyperelement’s documentation while the existing constructor accepts the attribute:

NoticeBox.variant('quiet', 'background: transparent; border-color: transparent;', doc='An unfilled notice without a visible border.')

NoticeBox.quiet [app] :is(notice-box)[quiet]: An unfilled notice without a visible border.



test_eq(list(NoticeBox.variants), ['quiet'])
to_xml(NoticeBox('Saved quietly.', quiet=True))

'<notice-box quiet>Saved quietly.</notice-box>'


To change a component only within part of a page, register an application rule scoped to that container. Here reg.rule registers editor-notices to square the corners of every notice-box inside an [editor] element, with an explicit name for later replacement. Because this rule is not registered on NoticeBox, it leaves the component’s definition untouched and appears in reg.layers['app'] rather than NoticeBox.rules:

reg.rule('[editor] notice-box { border-radius: 0; }', 'editor-notices', doc='Square notices inside the editor.')
reg.layers['app']

app-page [app]: A centered single-column page.
select-all [app] input[select-all]: Select the input text when it receives focus.
Field.base [app] label[field]: A labelled input
NoticeBox.corners [app] notice-box: Rounder notices in this application.
NoticeBox.quiet [app] :is(notice-box)[quiet]: An unfilled notice without a visible border.
editor-notices [app]: Square notices inside the editor.




Redefinitions
Calling hypelt again with the same name updates the hyperelement’s constructor and base rule in place, preserving existing references, application rules, and declared variants. Omitted css or on arguments are cleared rather than merged because the new call replaces the entire base rule. hypelt raises ValueError if sel changes because existing rules and variants are nested under the original root selector. Omitting on here makes NoticeBox persistent:

original, base = NoticeBox, NoticeBox.rules['base']
NoticeBox = hypelt('NoticeBox', css=lambda: notice_css.replace('8px', '12px'), layer='components', doc='A persistent notice.')
test_is(NoticeBox, original)
test_is(NoticeBox.rules['base'], base)
assert '12px' in base.compiled_css
assert 'corners' in NoticeBox.rules and 'quiet' in NoticeBox.variants
with expect_fail(ValueError): hypelt('NoticeBox', sel='notice-box[persistent]', css=notice_css, layer='components')
NoticeBox

NoticeBox(*children, **attrs)
A persistent notice.
Root selector: notice-box.
Declared variants: - quiet: An unfilled notice without a visible border.
Rules: - base (components) - corners (app): Rounder notices in this application.


The base rule now has no behaviors. To remove the application override, pass its full key to reg.remove. A layer view taken earlier no longer lists it:

test_eq(NoticeBox.behaviors, [])
app_rules = reg.layers['app']
v = reg.version
reg.remove('NoticeBox.corners')

NoticeBox.corners [app] notice-box: Rounder notices in this application.



assert 'NoticeBox.corners' not in app_rules
test_eq(reg.version, v+1)
app_rules
